Abstract— This study aims to assess pre-frailty stage of 
elderly using a Random Forest . The dataset consists of 
demography, physical function assessment tools, and gait 
analysis metrics from 121 participants. The Random Forest, 
optimized via random search and validated through 5-fold 
cross-validation, achieved an AUC (Area Under the Receiver 
Operating Characteristic Curve) of 0.78 ± 0. 06. Early 
identification using the proposed model enables prompt and 
targeted interventions, which are expected to potentially reduce 
the incidence of severe frailty and related ad verse health 
outcomes. 
Clinical Relevance— The findings of this study are relevant 
for clinicians involved in geriatric care, providing a reliable 
method to assess pre-frailty of elderly patients. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Frailty, characterized by a decline in physiological 
reserves and resistance to stressors, represents a critical 
challenge in geriatric health, predisposing elderly individuals 
to an increased risk of falls, hospitalization, disability, and 
mortality [1]. Frailty is often preceded by a transitional phase 
known as pre-frailty, which is marked by subtle impairments 
that may not yet fulfill the full diagnostic criteria of frailty but 
signal the onset of health deterioration [2]. Early detection and 
accurate classification of pre-frailty can facilitate timely and 
targeted interventions, thus delaying or preventing the onset of 
frailty and associated adverse health events. Therefore, in this 
study, we develop a classification model between healthy and 
pre-frailty elderly based on machine learning. 
II. METHODS 
In this study, we developed a classification model for 
pre-frailty using the GSTRIDE public dataset [3]. The dataset 
included a total of 46 features comprising demographic 
information (age, gender, height, weight, body mass index, 
and fall history), physical function assessment tools (4-meter 
gait walk test, short physical performance battery test, time Up 
and go test, and short falls efficacy scale international test), 
and gait analysis metrics collected from IMU (inertial 
measurement unit) sensors. The analysis involved 121 
participants, consisting of 62 healthy elderly individuals and

using a 5-fold cross-validation method. 
III. RESULTS 
Figure 1 illustrates the performance of the classification 
model developed in this study to differentiate between healthy 
elderly and pre-frail elderly. The asterisk (*) indicates the 
point of optimal sensitivity and specificity based on Youden's 
index. The model demonstrated a performance with an AUC 
of 0.78 ± 0.06 across the 5-fold cross-validation. 
 
Figure 1. ROC curves of the classification resuls between healthy and 
pre-frailty elderly using Random Forest. 
IV. DISCUSSION & CONCLUSION 
Integrating demographic data, physical function 
assessments, and gait analysis metrics with machine learning 
is anticipated to enhance our understanding of the pre-frailty 
stage in more detail. This result confirms the utility of machine 
learning in enhancing early detection and intervention 
strategies for geriatric diseases, ultimately alleviating the 
progression of frailty and improving health outcomes.
